changed_views: Mozilla's experience shifts the defensive-security question from whether a model can find bugs to the recurring cost of new-model sweeps and the organization's ability to validate and remediate them.
Agent-written software need not have a single ownership model: Mozilla explicitly separates human-readable community code from spec-and-test-driven regeneration.
Baseten's reported revenue remains dominated by differentiated customer models, even as stronger open models create demand for more standardized inference and additional behavioral safeguards.
follow_ups: Request Mozilla's vulnerability counts, severity distribution, independent reproduction rate, remediation time and actual versus credited token costs across successive model sweeps.
Inspect the Mozilla AI regenerated repositories and CQ implementation for test coverage, reproducibility, provenance, rollback and permission boundaries; green tests alone do not establish security.
Track Baseten's custom-model versus standard-API revenue mix and margins, and whether its partner-led guardrails become a supported product with explicit responsibility boundaries.
For Snorbl, verify how authored-content costs scale with library size and repeat use, and how keyword recognition, parental permissions and specialist content are validated with families.

signals.claim: Mozilla CTO Raffi Krikorian says Firefox has reached diminishing returns on the bugs its current Mythos access finds, while estimating full-codebase security runs would cost hundreds of thousands of dollars without supplied credits.
signals.evidence: Krikorian says Mozilla rapidly worked through Mythos findings, sometimes using the model to build a reproduction or testing harness rather than directly fix a bug. He explicitly avoids claiming all bugs are gone. Mozilla has received model access and credits; his hypothetical run cost is a back-of-envelope estimate, and he agrees repeated sweeps at the pace of new models could make that a monthly expense. He identifies slower-remediating infrastructure operators as a bigger concern than Firefox, not evidence of a specific breach.

signals.claim: Krikorian describes two different code-ownership contracts inside Mozilla: human review and commitment for Firefox, versus spec-driven regeneration of some entire codebases at Mozilla AI.
signals.evidence: He says Firefox allows agent-written code but requires a human to review, understand and stand behind each commit. At Mozilla AI, he reports some codebases have no human-written implementation: versioned specifications drive automated regeneration, with unit and end-to-end tests remaining green even as implementation bytes change frequently. Those tests establish the reported acceptance criterion, not a proof that regenerated software is correct or secure. Earlier, he describes CQ as a way to share agent discoveries and team workflow rules rather than have teammates independently recreate the same systems.

signals.claim: Baseten CTO Amir Haghighat says roughly 90% of revenue comes from serving customers' custom models, although adoption of its standard open-model APIs is increasing.
signals.evidence: Haghighat distinguishes customers that pretrain their own models, including Poolside, Inception and Cartesia, from customers that post-train existing models. He says the latter group also brings substantial validation work. He reports an uptick in the vanilla open-model API product after open models became useful for longer agent tasks, identifying June and GLM 5.2 as his perceived turning point. The revenue mix and adoption trend are company-reported; he supplies no absolute revenue, growth rate or profitability figures.

signals.claim: Haghighat separates the tenant-isolation boundary Baseten provides from the agent-behavior safeguards it currently leaves largely to customers and evaluation partners.
signals.evidence: He contrasts a basic container sandbox with VM or microVM isolation intended to keep one customer's code from accessing another customer's data. He does not claim this controls what the agent tries to do inside that boundary. Customers currently rely on their own model validation and partners such as Braintrust and LangChain; some accept single-tenant execution and blocked outbound networking. He expects a broader guardrail offering over time but describes it as a scope and prioritization decision, not an already-delivered end-to-end safety guarantee.

signals.claim: Snorbl CEO Mike Rizkalla reports about $20,000 per hour of authored content for its children's companion, using constrained language understanding and contextual triggers instead of open-ended generated dialogue.
signals.evidence: Rizkalla describes a small language model with a fixed intended role, a system for producing content with subject-matter experts, and keyword interpretation conditioned on context. He says parent-approved progression unlocks material as a child develops. His cost figure is content-production cost, not the price of an hour of customer usage. The approach deliberately purchases editorial control through authored material; proposed specialized family content and emotion-sensitive features are expansion plans, not demonstrated therapeutic effects or a blanket safety guarantee.

summary: The strongest material is first-party operating detail from Mozilla, Baseten and Snorbl, rather than the hosts' AGI and training-pause debate. Mozilla describes diminishing returns from one generation of security models and sharply different rules for agent-written code. Baseten distinguishes infrastructure isolation from agent-behavior safety while reporting that custom-model serving still supplies about 90% of revenue. Snorbl puts an explicit production cost on authored children's content instead of open-ended generation.
why_it_matters: These deployments expose costs and responsibilities hidden by capability demonstrations: repeated vulnerability sweeps require substantial inference budgets, passing tests does not settle human ownership of code, and an isolated runtime does not make an agent's actions safe. Baseten's revenue mix also cautions against treating the company as primarily a generic open-model API reseller, while Snorbl illustrates a content-production business model with deliberately constrained AI behavior.
